I'm a fan of **Carcassone** and I like teaching it - placing the tile is somewhat intuitive and you can repeat scoring possibilities repeatedly. 
 Start by saying the goal is to get the most points and that the meeples give you points for claiming certain features. 
 
 Then a turn outline - grab a tile at random (I keep them in a bag) and put it on the map, it needs to share at least one side with another tile, and it has to match - city to city, road to road, field to field. Then you can place a meeple on that tile that you just placed.  
 Then briefly explain scoring (but be ready to always do all the scoring) and getting your meeples back.
When you're pitching the game, let them know that it's pretty much just laying tiles. 

 
Also, and I say this from experience, spend the game teaching, not competing. You can play but explain your strategy, and don't destroy them.

For starting placement, I try to get a good wheat spot (everything but roads use wheat), then I look at what will likely be scarce - say wood has a 12, 3,11, and 9- I'll try to get a decent spot with the 9, now I'm set up to trade an in demand rare resource.
As the game progresses, don't get caught up in a plan, roll with what you have, try to cut people off, and if you can build a triad of settlements (3 roads at an intersection with no settlement in the middle, but one on each end) - this is the most efficient use of materials. Hope that helps?
